extracted.intended_audience: This American Life listeners, public radio audience, journalists and media professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for retracting a broadcast journalism piece: fact-checking, source verification, distinguishing theater from journalism, public correction, and accountability when a program cannot vouch for a story's truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vouch for the truth before broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Only air material for which the program can vouch for its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "We're retracting the story because we can’t vouch for its truth." If the program cannot confidently vouch for the factual accuracy of a piece, it should not be presented as journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous fact-checking and source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete and reliable fact-checking must be done before broadcast; verify claims and obtain verifiable contact information for sources and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During fact checking before the broadcast, This American Life staffers asked Daisey for this interpreter's contact information. Daisey lied to me and to This American Life producer Brian Reed during the fact checking we did on the story, before it was broadcast. "At that point, we should've killed the story."

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish journalism from theater
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate theatrical monologues or performances from reporting; do not present theater pieces as journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daisey: "it's not journalism. It's theater." If a piece is theatrical or a monologue, it must not be framed or broadcast as factual journalism without rigorous verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate anecdotal and geographic specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify concrete details such as locations, numbers, and specific incidents rather than relying on an interviewee's account alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some falsehoods were small (number of factories visited) and others large (claim that n-hexane poisoning occurred where Daisey said). Marketplace found the n-hexane incident occurred nearly a thousand miles away in Suzhou, not in Shenzhen where Daisey visited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond promptly to external reporting that raises doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: If other journalists or reporting raise credible questions about a story, investigate and, if necessary, correct or retract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Marketplace China correspondent tracked down the interpreter and disputed much of Daisey's account; This American Life devoted a program to detailing the errors after that external reporting raised issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly correct the record and explain errors
rubrics_metrics.description: When inaccuracies are found, publicly retract or correct the story, explain what was wrong, and provide supporting materials (press releases, transcripts, audio) so audiences can judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This American Life: "we will devote the entire hour to detailing the errors... A press release with more details about all this is below. We'll be posting the audio of the program and the transcript..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept responsibility and hold the program accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge institutional mistakes, express regret to the audience, and take concrete remedial actions tied to the program's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "That doesn't excuse the fact that we never should've put this on the air. In the end, this was our mistake." Actions included cancelling a live presentation and refunding tickets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold national journalistic standards and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to established journalistic standards for accuracy and integrity; failure to meet those standards undermines trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Our program adheres to the same journalistic standards as the other national shows, and in this case, we did not live up to those standards." Emphasizes reputation and trust in public radio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly distinguish verified facts from disputed material in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting or correcting a story, specify which parts were independently verified and which remain in dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "In our original broadcast, we fact checked all the things that Daisey said about Apple's operations in China... those parts of his story were true, except for the underage workers, who are rare. We reported that discrepancy in the original show."

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabrications and 'shortcuts' presented as firsthand experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow fabricated episodes, composite characters, or dramatized shortcuts to be presented as actual firsthand experiences in journalistic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daisey admitted to fabricating characters and shortcuts: "My mistake... is that I had it on your show as journalism, and it's not journalism. It's theater." Programs must ensure personal anecdotes are factual when presented as reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify identities and contactability of on-the-record witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain and independently verify the names and contact details of witnesses, interpreters, and other sources rather than relying on unverifiable claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This American Life staffers asked Daisey for the interpreter's contact information; Daisey provided misleading information (said her name was Anna, not Cathy, and that the cell number didn't work). Verifiable contact information enables corroboration.
